DLMS User Association: http://www.dlms.com.

133  Introduction – normative
134  The Gas Smart Metering Equipment Technical Specifications (GSMETS) requires that Gas
135  Smart Metering Equipment (GSME), and the Electricity Smart Metering Equipment Technical
136  Specifications (ESMETS) requires that Electricity Smart Metering Equipment (ESME) including
137  variants, meet the requirements described in the Great Britain Companion Specification
138  (GBCS).
139  ESME shall be certified by NCSC as compliant with a relevant version of the ‘Commercial
140  Product Assurance Security Characteristic Smart Metering – Electricity Smart Metering
141  Equipment’ as identified in the Smart Energy Code Section A.
142  GSME shall be certified by NCSC as compliant with a relevant version of the ‘Commercial
143  Product Assurance Security Characteristic Smart Metering – Gas Smart Metering Equipment’
144  as identified in the Smart Energy Code Section A.
145  The Communications Hub Technical Specifications (CHTS) requires that Communications
146  Hubs meet the requirements described in the GBCS.
147  A Communications Hub shall be certified by NCSC as compliant with a relevant version of the
148  ‘Commercial Product Assurance Security Characteristic Smart Metering - Communications
149  Hub’ as identified in the Smart Energy Code Section A.
150  The HAN Connected Auxiliary Load Control Switches (HCALCS) Technical Specifications
151  (HCALCSTS) requires that HCALCS meet the requirements described in the GBCS.

179 Structure of the GB Companion Specification (GBCS) and its relationship to other documents
180 – informative
181 The whole of this Section 2.2 is informative. A number of documents specify what Devices
182 should do and how they should do it, including:
183 the ‘Technical Specifications’ (GSMETS, ESMETS, SAPCTS IHDTS, HCALCSTS, PPMIDTS and
184 CHTS):
185 lay out minimum physical requirements and minimum functional capabilities for Devices;
186 specify that all Devices must use the ZSE protocol specifications; and
187 specify that Electricity Smart Metering Equipment (ESME) and SAPC must additionally use
188 DLMS COSEM protocol specifications.
189 International Standards documents, including those which lay out what is required to use
190 ZSE and DLMS COSEM protocols. However, the standards are flexible and could be used in
191 many different ways to implement technically the minimum functional requirements of the
192 Technical Specifications;
193 the end to end protocol that is defined in the GBCS, which deviates from the standard
194 ZigBee SEP and DLMS COSEM protocols in some instances. Suppliers and the DCC are
195 required to deploy Devices that are certified against those aspects of the GBCS that are fully
196 compliant with the ZigBee and DLMS COSEM protocols. Certification is not required against
197 those aspects of the GBCS where the ZigBee and DLMS COSEM protocols are actively dis-
198 applied or modified. For additional information on areas that would not require certification
199 please see Section 25 for ZigBee SEP, and Section 26 for DLMS COSEM.
200 GB Smart Metering requires technical interoperability, and so requires a single, consistent,
201 technical implementation of the capabilities laid out in the Technical Specifications across all
202 Devices, in so far as the network communications with Devices are concerned, be those
203 communications over the Smart Metering Home Area Network (SMHAN) or Wide Area
204 Network (WAN). The Devices in scope of this GBCS are:
205 Electricity Smart Metering Equipment (ESME), including Single Element, Polyphase, Twin
206 Element, Auxiliary Load Control Switch (ALCS), Auxiliary Proportional Controller (APC) and
207 Boost Function variants thereof;
208 Gas Smart Metering Equipment (GSME);
4 http://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc5912
Page 10

SEC Schedule 8 – GBCS v4.4
209 Communications Hub Function (CHF) and Communications Hub, Gas Proxy Function (GPF);
210 Standalone Auxiliary Proportional Controller (SAPC), including Auxiliary Load Control Switch
211 (ALCS) and Boost Function variants thereof;
212 Prepayment Interface Device (PPMID) and HAN Connected Auxiliary Load Control Switch
213 (HCALCS); and
214 Type 2 Devices, including In Home Displays (IHDs).
215 The purpose of this GBCS, and related documents, is to specify the single, consistent
216 technical implementation in sufficient detail to achieve operational interoperability of
217 Devices.
218 The Smart Metering technical and security architecture is based on a suite of agreed, open
219 standards, reflecting the UK Government strategy to facilitate the development of third
220 party innovative solutions for consumer devices. These include standards relating to DLMS
221 COSEM, ZSE, ASN.1, NIST cryptography and X.509 related IETF RFCs. The GBCS does not
222 duplicate what is laid out in such standards but rather provides references to them.
223 Scope and Terminology
224 Introduction – informative
225 This Section 3.1 is informative and summarises Section 3.
226 Section 3 introduces key terms used in the GBCS:
227 Messages are how Devices communicate between themselves and with organisations
228 remote from Consumers’ Premises. Such Messages are ‘end-to-end’ and ‘unicast’ in that:
229 they all identify the sender (e.g. a Supplier) and the intended recipient (e.g. an ESME); and
230 they are all intended for processing by the intended recipient, even though they may pass
231 through intermediate Devices, such as a Communications Hub Function. Most Messages
232 pass through Communications Hub Functions unaltered, save for any ‘wrapping’ information
233 needed for transport purposes. The only exceptions are where a CHF or GPF is the intended
234 recipient or is the sender (in these cases the Message is processed by the CHF or GPF), or
235 where covered by the Tapping Off Mechanism (Section 10);
236 Messages are one of:
237 a Command to a Device or a corresponding Response;
238 an Alert from a Device; or
239 an information provision transaction (HAN Only Message) solely between Devices;
Page 11

SEC Schedule 8 – GBCS v4.4
240 Organisations (such as Suppliers and Network Operators) communicating with Devices are
241 called Remote Parties;
242 Messages to and from Remote Parties are called Remote Party Messages; and
243 Messages solely between Devices are called HAN Only Messages.
244 Section 3 then:
245 explains that the GBCS only covers the Messages needed for the minimum functionality laid
246 out in the Technical Specifications;
247 explains that the GBCS specifies how all such Messages are constructed and related
248 processing performed; and
249 notes that Type 2 Devices (e.g. IHDs) can only send or receive HAN Only Messages.
250 Section 3 also explains some technical terminology and technical conventions used in this
251 GBCS.
252 Scope
253 This Section 3.2 lays out the scope of the GBCS and introduces definitions relied upon in this
254 GBCS.
255 A Message shall be of one the following:
256 a Command;
257 a Response to a Command;
258 an Alert; or
259 an information provision transaction (HAN Only Message).
260 A Message instance shall be an instance of one of the Messages detailed in this GBCS.
261 The Technical Specifications define the minimum functional capabilities required of Devices.
262 Except where those functional capabilities are internal to the Devices or are accessed via the
263 Device’s User Interfaces, the minimum functional capabilities shall be invoked by, and / or
264 result in, Messages being passed via the Devices’ Network Interfaces.
265 The GBCS is the technical specification, sufficient for the creation by the originator(s) and
266 processing by the target(s), of each Message, where the Message is required in order to
267 implement minimum functionality defined in the Technical Specifications.
268 Specifically, the GBCS details the format, structure and associated processing for each of the
269 Messages required to implement the Technical Specifications’ minimum functionality.
Page 12

SEC Schedule 8 – GBCS v4.4
270 There are two classifications of Message:
271 HAN Only Message5, where both the original sender and ultimate recipient are Devices
272 within the same Smart Metering Home Area Network (SMHAN); and
273 Remote Party Message, where either the original sender or the ultimate recipient is not a
274 Device.
275 A Remote Party Message shall only be of one of the following:
276 a Command;
277 a Response to a Command; or
278 an Alert.
279 Each Remote Party Message shall have a unique Message Code, which shall be as specified
280 in Section 15.
281 Where a Remote Party is known to a Device by way of that Remote Party’s Security
282 Credentials being stored on the Device (as specified in Section 4.3.2.5), the Remote Party is
283 referred to as a Known Remote Party (KRP). Otherwise, it is referred to as an Unknown
284 Remote Party (URP).
285 Commands requiring a Response to an Unknown Remote Party shall always be sent to the
286 Device by the Device’s Access Control Broker (see Section 4.3.2.5).
287 For clarity, Type 2 Devices shall not be required to support any Remote Party Messages.
288 Thus, provisions in this GBCS in relation to Remote Party Messages shall not apply to Type 2
289 Devices.
290 Remote Parties and Devices are collectively referred to in this GBCS as Smart Metering
291 Entities.
292 Terminology
293 Numbers
294 Numbers within this GBCS are expressed in one of three ways, to avoid potential ambiguity:
295 where a number has no prefix, it is a decimal number (base 10);
296 the 0x prefix is used for hexadecimal numbers (base 16). For example, 0x10 equates to the
297 decimal number 16; and
5 HAN Only Messages are ZigBee commands or response commands. This includes HAN
Only Messages passed between Devices using the ZSE TransferData, for example a
Command from a PPMID to a GSME.
Page 13

SEC Schedule 8 – GBCS v4.4
298 the 0b prefix is for binary numbers (base 2). For example, 0b1010 equates to the decimal
299 number 10.
300 Bit numbering
301 Numbering of bits uses the ‘LSB 0’ bit numbering scheme, where the least significant bit is
302 referred to as bit 0 and the most significant bit is referred to using the highest bit number.
303 Octets and bytes – informative
304 The term ‘octet’ is used to refer to units of 8 bits of digital information, to avoid potential
305 ambiguity with the term ‘byte’, and to align with protocol terminology.
306 An octet string is a sequence of octets, with the first octet shown on the left and the last
307 octet shown on the right, for example 0x12 0xAB 0x34 0xCD. If an octet string is shown
308 formatted as a hexadecimal number, the first octet is shown on the left (most significant)
309 and the last octet is shown on the right (least significant). For example, 0x12AB34CD used in
310 the context of an octet string represents 0x12 0xAB 0x34 0xCD.
311 Tag and MAC – informative
312 In this GBCS:
313 the word ‘tag’ is always used in the sense it is meant in encoding standards, such as A-XDR6
314 and Distinguished Encoding Rules (DER)7;
315 ‘tag’ is never used to mean Authentication tag, in the cryptographic sense;
316 ‘MAC’ is always used to mean Message Authentication Code, which is a cryptographic
317 checksum on data. Thus, MAC is used instead of Authentication tag; and
318 ‘MAC’ is never used to refer to Medium Access Control, as used in ‘MAC address’, which is a
319 unique identifier assigned to network interfaces.
320 Concatenation
321 X || Y shall mean the concatenation of the two octet strings X and Y.
322 For example:
323 X = 0xCAFE
324 Y = 0xBEEF
325 X || Y = 0xCAFEBEEF

SEC Schedule 8 – GBCS v4.4
326 Encoding and length of variable length unsigned integers
327 Encoding(X) shall be the encoding of a variable size unsigned integer X as follows:
328 if 0<X<128, then Encoding(X) is a single octet whose value is X; or
329 if 128<= X <256, then Encoding(X) is an octet string composed of the concatenation 0x81 ||
330 Y, where Y is one octet in length and has a value equal to X; or
331 if 256<= X <65,536, then Encoding(X) is an octet string composed of the concatenation 0x82
332 || Y, where Y is two octets in length and has a value equal to the big endian representation
333 of X; or
334 if 65,536<= X <16,777,216, then Encoding(X) is an octet string composed of the
335 concatenation 0x83 || Y, where Y is three octets in length and has a value equal to the big
336 endian representation of X.
337 Len(Encoding(X)) shall be the length in octets of Encoding(X).
338 GeneralizedTime
339 The GeneralizedTime ASN.1 type used in this GBCS shall be a UTC Time with a
340 resolution of one second. See section 46 of the ASN.1 specification for format.
341 Octet Endianness – Informative
342 Some fields (or elements) are one octet long, for example an 8 bit integer field.
343 Some fields are made up of more than one octet. For example a 16 bit integer is made up of
344 two octets. There are two ways of expressing these multiple octet elements, called ‘big
345 endian’ or ‘little endian’. Big endian means that the octets are listed from most significant
346 octet first to least significant octet last. Little endian is the reverse. Whether a field is
347 expressed as little or big endian is called endianness.
348 To illustrate, the decimal 500 can be represented as the hexadecimal value 0x01F4. As a 16
349 bit integer, its big endian representation is 0x01 then 0xF4 and its little endian
350 representation is 0xF4 then 0x01.
351 Endianness does not affect single octet elements, nor does it affect the sequence of
352 elements. Thus, it does not affect sequences of single octet elements such as 8 bit integer
353 arrays, byte arrays, octet strings or character strings.
354 The GBCS defaults to ‘big endian’ except for parts where a protocol specifies ‘little endian’
355 sequence.
356 The ZCL specification requires elements to be ‘little endian’ in ZCL commands. This applies to
357 all ZCL and ZSE commands, including those required by the GBCS (see Section 7.4 and
Page 15

SEC Schedule 8 – GBCS v4.4
358 elsewhere in the GBCS). It also applies to the ZCL header and ZCL payload parts of GBZ
359 Payloads, as required by Section 7.2. Note that all other elements of the GBZ Payloads, all
360 DLMS COSEM Payloads, all ASN.1 Security Payloads and all other parts of Messages
361 constructed according to Section 7.2 are ‘big endian’. This is because they are defined in the
362 GBCS and not in the ZCL specification. Thus, the GBZ Payload elements labelled ‘Profile ID’,
363 ‘Alert Code’, ‘Timestamp’, ‘Extended Header Cluster ID’, ‘Extended Header GBZ Command
364 Length’, ‘From Date Time’ and ‘Length of Ciphered Information’ are big endian. Note that the
365 GBZ Payload element ‘Ciphered Information’ is an octet string and so endianness is
366 irrelevant (since it is a sequence of single octet elements).
367 Note that GBCS does not use the two octet ‘Manufacturer code’ field in the ZCL Header. The
368 other three fields in the ZCL Header are single octet elements and so endianness has no
369 effect in relation to ZCL Header.
370 Security
371 Introduction – informative
372 This Section 4.1 is informative and summarises Section 4.
373 Section 4.2 lays out security provisions that are common across Messages, specifically
374 stating that:
375 at the application layer, all Messages must have integrity and authenticity protections,
376 Critical Messages must have non-repudiation protections and some parts of Messages must
377 have Confidentiality protections applied to specific data content; and
378 ZSE protections will be relied upon when Devices within the same Smart Metering Home
379 Area Network (SMHAN) communicate with each other.
380 Section 4.3 lays out security provisions that are common across Remote Party Messages,
381 specifically:
382 Identifiers, Counters and Protection Against Replay: lays out requirements in relation to
383 identifiers, counters and their use in Protection Against Replay;
384 Security Credentials: lays out requirements for all Devices, except for Type 2 Devices, to:
385 have Public-Private Key Pairs, and to make their Public Keys available; and
386 have Trust Anchor Cells, including those which are storage areas within a Device, capable of
387 holding Public Key Security Credentials for a number of Remote Parties, with the set of
388 Remote Parties being derived from the functionality the Device supports; and
389 Cryptographic Primitives and their Usage: lays out requirements for Cryptographic
390 Algorithms and their usage, in relation to Remote Party Messages.
Page 16

SEC Schedule 8 – GBCS v4.4
391 Note that the cryptographic protections are intentionally independent of whether a
392 Message Payload is structured according to the ZSE, ASN.1 or DLMS COSEM standards. This
393 means that Suppliers, Network Operators, the Access Control Broker and Other Users who
394 may communicate with Devices need only implement cryptographic requirements in one
395 way, regardless of the type of Device they are communicating with.
396 The same requirements for security apply regardless of whether a Message is delivered by
397 the Wide Area Network (WAN), SMHAN, Hand Held Terminal (HHT) or local interface. Note
398 that, for Prepayment Top Up, there are a number of different Messages. The content of
399 each particular Message will always be processed in the same way regardless of delivery
400 mechanism.
401 The following additional points are to be noted:
402 the governance and structures to ensure uniqueness of identifiers are set out in the Smart
403 Energy Code (SEC) and are outside the scope of the GBCS.
404 a single Originator Counter can be used for the whole of a Remote Party Organisation (e.g.
405 by that Party counting small enough time intervals). A separate counter per Device is not
406 required;
407 the Supplementary Originator Counter as specified in Section 4.3.1.4 is required where the
408 corresponding Response has to be cryptographically protected (by way of both Encryption
409 and a MAC), to the Supplementary Remote Party. In all other cases, the Response
410 containing Supplementary Remote Party details is protected back to the Access Control
411 Broker; and
412 Smart Metering entities make extensive use of a range of Counters as part of the unique
413 identification of Smart Metering Messages. Counters are also a key component used to
414 support Protection Against Replay functionality.
415 Cryptographic Protections applying to all Messages
416 Each Message shall have Cryptographic Protections to give assurance to the Message
417 recipient(s) as to:
418 the Message’s integrity; and
419 the Authenticity of the party or parties creating or augmenting the Message.
420 The minimum set of such Cryptographic Protections is laid out in this GBCS.
421 This GBCS lays out the Cryptographic Protections for non-repudiation, where this quality is
422 required for specific Messages, so for Critical Messages.

424 ensure both its Confidentiality and its integrity, as detailed in this GBCS.
425 For HAN Only Messages the Cryptographic Protections required by this GBCS shall be those
426 provided by ZSE.

514 Security Credentials
515 Introduction – informative
516 A Device shall be able to process four kinds of Security Credential Document:
517 its own Security Credential Documents, provided in the form of Device Certificates. Here the
518 Device needs processing to cover (1) generating new Public-Private Key Pairs and so issuing
519 Device Certification Requests, (2) storing its Device Certificates and (3) providing a copy of
520 those Device Certificates on request;
521 Security Credential Documents relating to Known Remote Parties, provided in the form of
522 Organisation Certificates. For these, the Device needs to be capable of (1) storing, (2)
523 replacing and (3) providing details of those it holds on request;
Page 21

SEC Schedule 8 – GBCS v4.4
524 Security Credential Documents relating to Unknown Remote Parties, provided in the form of
525 Organisation Certificates. For these, the Device will receive them in a Command so that
526 parts of the Response can be Encrypted. The Device does not need to store such
527 Documents; and
528 Security Credential Documents relating to Certification Authorities, provided in the form of
529 Certification Authority Certificates. These are processed by the Device only when replacing
530 Remote Parties’ Security Credential Documents.
531 Sections 8 and 13 cover the above functionality.
532 Section 12 covers requirements related to the structure and content of such Security
533 Credential Documents, where such requirements are relevant to Device processing
534 requirements.
535 This Section 4.3.2 covers requirements for the storage of such Security Credentials on
536 Devices and their usage in verifying cryptographic protections on Commands the Device
537 receives.
538 Security Credential Documents
539 A Security Credential Document shall be either:
540 a Device Certificate; or
541 a Remote Party’s Organisation Certificate; or
542 a Certification Authority Certificate.
543 Device Certificate
544 A Device Certificate shall relate to only one Device and shall meet the requirements
545 specified at Section 12. A Device Certificate shall either be used for Key Agreement or
546 Digital Signing but not both. Device Certificates shall only be issued by Authorised Public
547 Key Infrastructure (APKI) issuing Certification Authority. Where Security Credentials relating
548 to a Device are incorporated in a Message, the Security Credentials shall be incorporated in
549 the Message in the form of the Device Certificate.
550 Remote Party’s Certificate
551 A Remote Party Certificate shall be one of that Remote Party’s Organisation Certificates and
552 so shall relate to only one Remote Party and shall meet the requirements specified at
553 Section 12. As per Section 12, except where remotePartyRole = root a Remote Party
554 Certificate shall either be used for Key Agreement or Digital Signing but not both. Remote
555 Party Certificates shall only be issued by APKI authorised issuing Certification Authorities.
556 Where Security Credentials relating to a Remote Party are incorporated in a Message, the
Page 22

SEC Schedule 8 – GBCS v4.4
557 Security Credentials shall be incorporated in the Message in the form of the Remote Party’s
558 Certificate.
559 Certification Authority Certificate
560 A Certification Authority Certificate shall relate to only one Certification Authority and shall
561 meet the requirements specified at Section 12. A Certification Authority Certificate shall
562 only be used by a Device for verifying Digital Signatures on Certificates. Where Security
563 Credentials relating to a Certification Authority are incorporated in a Message, the Security
564 Credentials shall be incorporated in the Message in the form of the Certification Authority’s
565 Certificate.
566 Device Security Credentials
567 Where a Device is of deviceType that is gSME, eSME8,
568 communicationsHubCommunicationsHubFunction, or
569 communicationsHubGasProxyFunction, that Device shall have the capacity to store and
570 use securely four private keys:
571 for Key Agreement, a Current Private Key and a Pending Private Key; and
572 for Digital Signing, a Current Private Key and a Pending Private Key.
573 Where a Device is of deviceType that is type1HANConnectedAuxiliaryLoadControlSwitch or
574 type1PrepaymentInterfaceDevice, that Device shall have the capacity to store and use
575 securely two private keys:
576 for Key Agreement, a Current Private Key; and
577 for Digital Signing, a Current Private Key.
578 These stores shall be referred to as Private Key Cells.
579 Wherever one of a Device’s Private Keys is required to be used by a GBCS Cryptographic
580 Protection process, only the relevant Current Private Key shall be used. A Device shall not
581 use any Pending Private Key in any GBCS Cryptographic Protection.
582 Where a Device holds a Private Key that is to be used for Key Agreement, the corresponding
583 Public-Private Key Pair shall have been generated according to the section B.4.1 of FIPS 186-
584 49 using the ‘ECC Key Pair Generation Using Extra Random Bits’ method.

668 Agreement Private Key.
669 All other MACs in Commands shall be verified using the Public Key in Trust Anchor Cell
670 {remotePartyRole accessControlBroker, keyUsage keyAgreement, cellUsage management},
671 along with the Device’s Key Agreement Private Key.
672 Signature
673 Where a Command has a Digital Signature, the Device shall identify the Remote Party Role(s)
674 which can legitimately sign the Command according to the message code identified in the
675 Mapping Table.
676 If there is only one Remote Party Role so identified, then the signature shall be verified using
677 the Public Key in Trust Anchor Cell {remotePartyRole (the identified remote party role),
678 keyUsage digitalSignature, cellUsage management}.
679 If there is more than one Remote Party Role so identified, the Device shall use the Business
680 Originator ID in the Command to identify the Trust Anchor Cell(s) where:
681 keyUsage = digitalSignature;
682 cellUsage = management; and
683 existingSubjectUniqueID = the Business Originator ID in the Command
684 If there is only one Trust Anchor Cell so identified, then the signature shall be verified using
685 the Public Key in that Trust Anchor Cell.
686 If there is more than one Trust Anchor Cell so identified the Device shall attempt to verify
687 the Digital Signature using each Trust Anchor Cell identified. These attempts shall be
688 according to the following precedence, and attempts to verify shall cease when a signature
689 verification succeeds:
690 supplier;
691 wanProvider;
692 networkOperator;

693 accessControlBroker.
694 For clarity, other Remote Party Roles on Devices are limited to Commands related to Security
695 Credentials and so cannot have Trust Anchor Cells identified according to this Section
696 4.3.2.7.2.
697 Certification Path Validation
698 Access Control Broker requirements
699 Before it calculates the Access Control Broker to Device MAC (ACB-SMD MAC) in line with
700 Section 6.2.3, the Access Control Broker shall undertake Certification Revocation List (CRL)
701 Validation for any Organisation Certificate in a Command:
702 either by using the algorithm specified in IETF RFC 528013 section 6.3; or
703 by using functionality equivalent to the external behaviour resulting from that algorithm.
704 Only if the CRL Validation is successful shall the Access Control Broker calculate the ACB-
705 SMD MAC. For clarity, the Access Control Broker shall never send a Message to a Device
706 which contains any Certificate that has failed CRL Validation.
707 Device requirements
708 The requirements in this Section 4.3.2.8.2 shall apply only to Use Cases CS02b (Update
709 Security Credentials) and CS02g (Update Load Controller Security Credentials).
710 Where a Device has successfully completed all required Command Authenticity and Integrity
711 checks on a Command, of a type covered by Use Cases CS02b and CS02g, the Device shall
712 undertake either:
713 Certification Path Validation, including time checks; or
714 Certification Path Validation, excluding time checks.
715 If the Device does not have Reliable Time (as defined in Use Cases GCS28 and ECS70 Set
716 Clock) it shall always undertake Certification Path Validation, excluding time checks.
717 Otherwise the validation to be undertaken shall be determined by the contents of the
718 Remote Party Command instance. For clarity, Device types which are not required to have a
719 clock, shall always undertake Certification Path Validation, excluding time checks.
720 The Device shall undertake Certification Path Validation, including time checks:
721 either by using the algorithm specified in IETF RFC 5280 section 6.1; or
722 by using functionality equivalent to the external behaviour resulting from that algorithm.
13 http://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc5280/

SEC Schedule 8 – GBCS v4.4
723 The Device shall undertake Certification Path Validation, excluding time checks:
724 either by using the algorithm specified in IETF RFC 5280 section 6.1 but not applying the
725 check at 6.1.3 (a) (2) (‘the certificate validity period includes the current time’); or
726 by using functionality equivalent to the external behaviour resulting from that algorithm
727 where not applying the check that ‘the certificate validity period includes the current time’.
728 For clarity, Certification Path Validation shall only apply to replacement Certificates in the
729 Command, not to an existing Certificate in a Trust Anchor cell.
730 The ‘trust anchor’ information (with the meaning in IETF RFC 5280) shall be in the root
731 Security Credentials held on the Device.
732 If the Device’s Certificate Path Validation does not confirm the required certification path
733 validity, then the Device shall undertake no further processing of the Command, except for
734 the issuance of a Message containing an executionOutcome (with its Section 13.3.4.6
735 meaning) notifying that the Command was unsuccessful in applying at least some of the
736 changes in the Command.
737 DLMS Client and Server
738 The Access Control Broker shall perform the role of DLMS COSEM client in relation to the
739 DLMS COSEM Application Associations, and the Device shall perform the role of DLMS
740 COSEM server.
741 Cryptographic primitives and their usage
742 In relation to any Remote Party Message, Smart Metering Entities shall:
743 use SHA-256, as specified in FIPS 180-414, as the Hash function;
744 use the AES-128 cipher, as specified in FIPS 19715, as the block cipher primitive;
745 use the Galois Counter Mode (GCM) mode of operation as specified in NIST Special
746 Publication 800-38D16 ;
747 use the GMAC technique, based on the use of AES-128, for the calculation of Message
748 Authentication Codes (MACs), as specified in NIST Special Publication 800-38D (see above);

753 Agreement technique (as specified in NIST Special Publication 800-56Ar217 save for the

755 the Single-step Key Derivation Function (KDF) based on SHA-256, as specified in NIST Special

758 Resulting DerivedKeyingMaterial (with its meaning in NIST Special Publication 800-56Ar2)
759 shall only ever be used in relation to one Message instance. Any Shared Secret that is not

761 Scope of Cryptographic Protections
762 The fields that shall always contribute to MAC and Digital Signature are detailed in Section
763 7.2. Fields that vary across Messages are specified in Section 6, and in the relevant Use
764 Cases. For clarity, a Message instance may transit through multiple Smart Metering Entities
765 before delivery to its target Device, and more than one Smart Metering Entity may be
766 required to apply a Cryptographic Protection to that Message instance. Thus, the scope of
767 protection can only be across fields in the Message instance as constructed at the point the
768 protection is applied.
769 Where a Message has multiple Cryptographic Protections, the order in which the Smart
770 Metering Entities apply these Cryptographic Protections is specified in this GBCS.
771 A Device verifying the Cryptographic Protections in such Messages shall undertake such
772 verifications in the reverse sequence to that in which the Cryptographic Protections were
773 applied. This order is also specified in this GBCS.
774 ECDSA per message secret number
775 When generating a Digital Signature, the Smart Metering Entity shall calculate the DSA Per-
776 Message Secret Number ‘k’ with respect to ECDSA (with the meaning in section 6.3 of FIPS
777 186-4) to be the SHA-256 hash of the concatenation of:
778 the parts of the Message to be signed, as defined in Section 7.2.7; and
779 the Private Key that the Smart Metering Entity will use in the Digital Signature generation.

780 If the value of k so calculated is zero or greater than n -1, or results in an ‘r’ or ‘s’ value of 0,

785 and

791 Calculating unique Shared Secret Keys for a Remote Party Message Instance
792 Where a Smart Metering Entity executes the KDF in relation to a Message instance, the

794 using the value of information provided in, or to be placed in, the originator-system-title,

796 requirements of Section 7.2.7.
797 The OtherInfo shall be in the Concatenation Format as defined in section 5.8.1.2.1 of NIST
798 Special Publication 800-56Ar2 and shall be the concatenation:
799 AlgorithmID || value of originator-system-title || length of transaction-id || value of
800 transaction-id || value of recipient-system-title

802 AlgorithmID is that for AES-GCM-128 and so has a value 0x60857406080300, as specified by
803 section 9.2.3.4.6.5 of the Green Book; and
804 length of transaction-id has the value 0x09.

806 In relation to Remote Party Messages, Smart Metering Entities shall use a 96 bit Initialization
807 Vector (IV) for the GCM and GMAC algorithms as defined in NIST Special Publication 800-38D.
808 The IV shall be the concatenation:
809 FixedField || InvocationField

833 Common Message Structures – informative
834 Parts of the structure and content of Remote Party Messages are common across multiple
835 Remote Party Messages. These common parts of the structure and content are laid out in
836 Section 7 of this GBCS. Section 7 also lays out specific requirements for DLMS COSEM and
837 ZSE compliance for Devices compliant with this GBCS.
838 Note that Remote Party Messages in this GBCS are all constructed using aggregation
839 structures. The GBCS does not allow for more granular message structures (e.g. for DLMS
840 COSEM, individual set, get or action messages).
841 Common Encryption and Decryption approach – informative
842 The content and processing of fields in relation to Confidentiality shall be common across all
843 parts of Messages requiring such protections. Where specified in a Use Case, a Remote
844 Party Message may contain one or more encrypted parts. For such requirements, the
845 corresponding Authenticated Encryption and Authenticated Decryption shall always be
846 undertaken using the approach laid out in Section 8.
847 Note that the GBCS does not require Encryption of the whole of a Message.
848 Message Categories – informative
849 The content and processing of fields related to integrity, authenticity and non-repudiation
850 varies according to whether:
851 the Message is a Command, Response or Alert; and
852 the Message is a Critical Message or not.
853 This leads to groupings which are referred to as Message Categories. Message Categories
854 are structured in a hierarchical way, with the more generally applicable categories being at
855 the tiers of the hierarchy with lower numbers. A category which is derived from another
856 category (i.e. in a tier with a higher number) is called a subordinate Message Category. A
857 category from which another category is derived (i.e. in a tier with a lower number) is called
858 a superordinate Message Category. Figure 5.3 summarises the hierarchy.

1259  Message structure and DLMS COSEM / ZSE / ASN.1 requirements
1260  Introduction – informative
1261  This Section 7:
1262  defines the structure of Remote Party Messages containing DLMS COSEM, ASN.1 and GBZ
1263  Payloads.  A GBZ Payload is a Payload containing one or more ZigBee messages;
1264  defines the structure of Messages between a PPMID and a GSME on the same SMHAN; and
|     |     |     |     | Page 57  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | -------- |

SEC Schedule 8 – GBCS v4.4
1265 lays out specific requirements for DLMS COSEM and ZigBee compliance to which Devices
1266 shall adhere.
1267 Note that Remote Party Messages all use an aggregation structure which allows for multiple,
1268 protocol-specific instructions within the same Message. The aggregation structures are used
1269 for all Messages, are based on DLMS COSEM access service, general signing service and
1270 general ciphering service formats, and provide protections across all types of Message
1271 payload (be they DLMS COSEM, ZSE or security related).
1272 The GBCS does not provide more granular Message structures (e.g. for DLMS COSEM,
1273 individual set, get or action messages).
1274 The Technical Specifications require that the Critical Commands mandated by them (and so
1275 those defined in the GBCS) are the only Critical commands allowed. Devices may implement
1276 additional non Critical features only.
1277 It should be noted that:
1278 SMETS only requires DLMS COSEM certification on the ESME and the SAPC;
1279 any action that the Known Remote Party takes to remedy a failure will need to factor in that
1280 some of the instructions succeeded and others did not;
1281 in ASN.1 notation, the signature field in the general-signing service is a variable length
1282 OCTET STRING. When encoded, this means that the length of the signature needs to be
1283 incorporated before the actual signature value. The length is either 64 (0x40) if a signature
1284 is present or 0 (0x00) if signature is not present;
1285 these requirements are to ensure that all Devices behave consistently and in the way
1286 required by originating Remote Party requests, including in error states; and
1287 the WAN Provider may read CHF Operational Data and CHF Configuration Data, with their
1288 CHTS meanings, using mechanisms other than those defined in this GBCS.
1289 Remote Party Message construction – general
1290 This Section 7.2 shall apply to Messages which are of a Message Category that is not
1291 ‘Variant’. For Messages of a Message Category that is ‘Variant’, this Section 7.2 shall only
1292 apply where explicitly stated in the Use Case, with the exception of Section 7.2.11 which
1293 shall apply to all Messages.
1294 Except for elements detailed as being defined in the ZSE or ZCL specifications, the octet
1295 strings constructed in compliance with this Section 7 shall be in ‘big endian’ order according
1296 to IETF RFC 170019. Elements detailed in this Section 7 as being defined in the ZSE or ZCL
19 http://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc1700
Page 58

SEC Schedule 8 – GBCS v4.4
1297 specifications, shall be serialised into the corresponding parts of octet strings as defined in
1298 the corresponding ZSE or ZCL specification.
1299 Commands
1300 Whether a Command requires a KRP Signature is specified in the corresponding Message
1301 Category requirements in Section 6.
1302 Where a KRP Signature is required, a Remote Party Command received by a Device shall be
1303 the concatenation:
1304 MAC Header || Grouping Header || Command Payload || 0x40 || KRP Signature || ACB-
1305 SMD MAC
1306 Where a KRP Signature is not required, a Remote Party Command received by a Device shall
1307 be the concatenation:
1308 MAC Header || Grouping Header || Command Payload || 0x00 || ACB-SMD MAC
1309 A HAN Only Command from a PPMID to a GSME shall be the concatenation:
1310 MAC Header || Grouping Header || Command Payload || 0x00 || PPMID-GSME MAC
1311 Responses
1312 Whether a Response requires an SMD Signature is specified in the corresponding Message
1313 Category requirements in Section 6.
1314 Where a SMD Signature is required, a Remote Party Response shall be the concatenation:
1315 Grouping Header || Response Payload || 0x40 || SMD Signature
1316 Where a SMD Signature is not required, a Remote Party Response shall be the
1317 concatenation:
1318 MAC Header || Grouping Header || Response Payload || 0x00 || SMD-KRP MAC
1319 A HAN Only Response from a GSME to a PPMID shall be the concatenation:
1320 MAC Header || Grouping Header || Response Payload || 0x00 || GSME-PPMID MAC
1321 Alerts
1322 Whether an Alert requires an SMD Signature is specified in the corresponding Message
1323 Category requirements in Section 6.
1324 Where a SMD Signature is required, a Remote Party Alert shall be the concatenation:
1325 Grouping Header || Alert Payload || 0x40 || SMD Signature
1326 Where a SMD Signature is not required, a Remote Party Alert shall be the concatenation:

1327 MAC Header || Grouping Header || Alert Payload || 0x00 || SMD-KRP MAC
1328 Payload sequence and Break On Error
1329 All Message Payloads - Command Payloads, Response Payloads and Alert Payloads - shall:
1330 only be constructed in the sequence specified in the corresponding Use Case;
1331 only be processed in the sequence specified in the corresponding Use Case; and
1332 be processed by a recipient Device on a Break On Error basis.
1333 Where a Command Payload contains multiple instructions, processing of further instructions
1334 shall cease at the point any one instruction fails. In line with the DLMS COSEM Access
1335 Services requirements, a Response shall contain one result for each instruction in the
1336 Command, except where the instruction in the Command is a ZSE GetDayProfiles or
1337 GetWeekProfiles command where one or more ZSE commands may be produced in the
1338 Response in line with the ZSE specification. The corresponding result in the Response
1339 Payload shall detail that instruction's success or failure. The Response Payload shall
1340 explicitly detail a result for each of the subsequent instructions that were not attempted.
1341 The results in the Response shall be in the same order as the instructions in the Command.
1342 The specific result codes shall be as specified in the relevant ZSE / DLMS COSEM document
1343 or in this GBCS where standard-based error codes do not exist. Where execution of
1344 instructions was not attempted due to the Break On Error requirement, the response shall
1345 return:
1346 for DLMS instructions, a Data-Access-Result / Action-Result of other-reason;
1347 for each such ZCL / ZSE instruction, a Default Response command where the ZCL payload
1348 status field has a value of FAILURE (0x01), ZCL payload Command ID is set to 0xFF and the
1349 ZCL header Frame Control field is set to 0x00 or 0x08, with the Direction Sub-field being 0b0
1350 or 0b1 in line with the ZigBee specifications.
1351 A ZSE command returning a status of ‘NOT_FOUND’ shall not be treated as a failure.

SEC Schedule 8 – GBCS v4.4
1491 A GBT Message Series shall be the set of GBT Messages needed to exchange one complete
1492 Remote Party Message between a GBT Initiator and a GBT Recipient.
1493 For a Remote Party Command sent using a GBT Message Series, the GBT Initiator shall be the
1494 Access Control Broker, or the HHT for Remote Party Commands delivered via the HHT and
1495 the GBT Recipient shall be the target Device.
1496 For a Remote Party Response or a Remote Party Alert sent using a GBT Message Series, the
1497 GBT Initiator shall be the sending Device and the GBT Recipient shall be the Access Control
1498 Broker and the HHT where such Remote Party Messages are also delivered to the HHT in line
1499 with the requirements of Section 10.5.3.2.
1500 A GBT Third Party shall be the Remote Party identified by:
1501 in a Remote Party Command, the value in the Business Originator ID field; and
1502 in a Remote Party Response or a Remote Party Alert, the value in the Business Target ID field.
1503 GBT Streaming Window shall be the number of GBT Messages the GBT Initiator sends
1504 without receipt of a GBT Message (Acknowledgement), or since receipt of the most recent
1505 GBT Message (Acknowledgement).
1506 GBT Streaming Window shall be:
1507 63 where the GBT Message Series carries a Remote Party Response;
1508 6 where the GBT Message Series carries a Remote Party Command; or
1509 the number of GBT Messages the sender wishes to be resent in response to a GBT Message
1510 (Request Block Resend).
1511 Maximum PDU Size shall be 1200 octets.
1512 For clarity, recovery of lost blocks may take place before the end of the streaming window.
1513 Remote Party Message size
1514 Where a Remote Party Message exceeds the Maximum PDU Size, the GBT Initiator and the
1515 GBT Responder shall exchange the Remote Party Message in a GBT Message Series.
1516 Where a Remote Party Message does not exceed the Maximum PDU Size, the GBT Initiator
1517 and the GBT Responder may exchange the Remote Party Message in a GBT Message Series.
1518 GBT Message Structure
1519 A GBT Message shall, if it is a GBT Message (Acknowledgement) or a GBT Message (Request
1520 Block Resend), be the concatenation:
1521 Message Routing Header || GBT Header
Page 83

SEC Schedule 8 – GBCS v4.4
1522 A GBT Message shall, if it is neither a GBT Message (Acknowledgement) nor a GBT Message
1523 (Request Block Resend), be the concatenation:
1524 Message Routing Header || GBT Header || GBT Block Data
1525 where:
1526 Message Routing Header shall be structured and populated according to Table 7.2.11.5.
1527 Note that Message Routing Header (1) uniquely identifies the GBT Message Series, (2)
1528 identifies whether the GBT Message is being sent to or from the Device and (3)
1529 unambiguously ties all GBT Messages in the GBT Message Series to the single Remote Party
1530 Message being exchanged;
1531 GBT Header shall be structured and populated according to Table 7.2.11.6; and
1532 GBT Block Data shall be the part of the Remote Party Message, constructed as per Section
1533 7.2.11.4, being carried in this GBT Message.
1534 GBT Message processing
1535 The GBT Initiator shall, once the Remote Party Message is fully constructed and all
1536 cryptographic protections are applied, slice the octet string produced so that:
1537 1. GBT Block Data with GBT Initiator Block Number of 1 is the 1149 most significant octets
1538 of the Remote Party Message, or all of the octets if the size of the Remote Party
1539 Message is less than 1149 octets;
1540 2. GBT Block Data with GBT Initiator Block Number of 2 is the next 1149 most significant
1541 octets of the Remote Party Message, or all of the octets if the size of the remaining
1542 octets in Remote Party Message is less than 1149 octets; and
1543 3. remaining GBT Block Data are created by repeating Step 2, each time incrementing GBT
1544 Initiator Block Number by 1, until there are no remaining octets in the Remote Party
1545 Message.
1546 The GBT Recipient shall not undertake any processing, in the sense of Section 6, of the
1547 Remote Party Message carried in a GBT Message Series until it has received:
1548 a GBT Message in this GBT Message Series where the ‘last-block’ field contains 0b1 (meaning
1549 last block); and
1550 all GBT Messages in this GBT Message Series with ‘block-number’ fields less than the ‘block-
1551 number’ field in the last block. Where the GBT Recipient has not received all such GBT
1552 Messages, it shall send a GBT Message (Request Block Resend) for each missing block-
1553 number. Where the GBT Recipient is a Device, it may discard all blocks in a GBT Message
Page 84

SEC Schedule 8 – GBCS v4.4
1554 Series if it has received no response to a GBT Message (Request Block Resend) after 60
1555 minutes.
1556 For clarity, the GBT Recipient may, where it is a Device, immediately discard, without any
1557 further processing, any GBT Message where:
1558 the Message Code in the Message Routing Header is for a Command, which requires
1559 Protection Against Replay; and
1560 the Device’s Execution Counter, for the Business Originator ID and Message Code specified in
1561 the Message Routing Header, is equal to or greater than the Originator Counter in the
1562 Message Routing Header
1563 When a GBT Message Series carries a Response and that GBT Message Series consists of
1564 more than 63 GBT Messages, the GBT Recipient shall, if it wishes to receive all parts of the
1565 GBT Message Series, send a GBT Message (Acknowledgement) when it has received each
1566 complete set of 63 sequential GBT Messages. Note, when the Device sending the Response
1567 receives such a GBT Message (Acknowledgement), it is able to begin sending the next
1568 sequence of GBT Messages in the GBT Message Series.
1569 GBT Recipient Block Number shall be set to 0x0001 in the first GBT Message sent by the GBT
1570 Recipient. It shall be incremented by 1 in each subsequent GBT Message it sends.
1571 GBT Initiator Block Number Ack shall be the highest of:
1572 0x0000; and
1573 the highest block-number in any GBT Message the GBT Initiator has received in this GBT
1574 Message Series.
1575 GBT Recipient Block Number Ack shall:
1576 in a GBT Message (Acknowledgement), be the highest block-number in any GBT Message the
1577 GBT Recipient has received in this GBT Message Series; and
1578 in a GBT Message (Request Block Resend), the value of block-number up to which the GBT
1579 Recipient has received all the prior numbered GBT Messages in this GBT Message Series.
1580 Where the GBT Initiator is a Device, the Device shall be able to resend any GBT Message
1581 within a GBT Message Series, for a minimum period from when it sends the first GBT
1582 Message in that series, to whichever is the sooner of:
1583 it receiving an authenticated GBT Message (Acknowledgement) where the GBT Recipient
1584 Block Number Ack contains a value equal to the highest value of GBT Initiator Block Number
1585 in this GBT Message Series; or
1586 24 hours later.

1588  sense of Section 6.  For example, the following GBT Messages would be malformed:
1589  one with ‘block-number’ equal to zero (this does not comply with the GBCS); and

1592  Where the GBT Recipient is an ESME or an SAPC, the Device shall not send a GBT Message

1595  minutes elapse without the Device receiving corresponding GBT Message(s) in response, the
1596  Device may discard the GBT Messages it has received in this GBT Message Series.

1600 Table 7.2.11.6: GBT Header
1601 Illustrations – informative
1602 GBT allows for the transport of Messages where the Message is greater than the Maximum
1603 PDU Size. A number of Use Cases can result in this larger Message size, either as a
1604 Command or a Response. There are no Alert Use Cases that result in the larger Message size.
1605 GBT does not change any part of the Remote Party Message content that is being
1606 transported.
1607 Example 1: A small Command with small Response – e.g. read MPAN.
1608 Without GBT, the Command is:
1609 MAC Header || Grouping Header || read MPAN Command Payload || 0x00 || ACB-SMD
1610 MAC
1611 and the Response is:
1612 MAC Header || Grouping Header || read MPAN Response Payload || 0x00 || SMD-KRP
1613 MAC
Page 89

SEC Schedule 8 – GBCS v4.4
1614 GBT can be applied to this Use Case. The Command becomes:
1615 Message Routing Header || GBT Header || MAC Header || Grouping Header || read MPAN
1616 Command Payload || 0x00 || ACB-SMD MAC
1617 and the Response becomes:
1618 Message Routing Header || GBT Header || MAC Header || Grouping Header || read MPAN
1619 Response Payload || 0x00 || SMD-KRP MAC
1620 Example 2: A large Command with small Response – e.g. set tariff on an ESME where the
1621 tariff is complex.
1622 Without GBT, the Command is:
1623 MAC Header || Grouping Header || set Tariff Command Payload || 0x40 || KRP Signature
1624 || ACB-SMD MAC
1625 For the purposes of example, assume this is divided into three blocks, so block-numbers 1, 2
1626 and 3. Actual set tariff Commands will vary from this number of blocks.
1627 The Command is transmitted as the GBT Message Series:
1628 Message Routing Header || GBT Header || block 1
1629 Message Routing Header || GBT Header || block 2
1630 Message Routing Header || GBT Header || block 3
1631 This is reconstructed at the ESME, by concatenating blocks 1, 2 and 3 to give:
1632 MAC Header || Grouping Header || set Tariff Command Payload || 0x40 || KRP Signature
1633 || ACB-SMD MAC
1634 The Response could have the following structure:
1635 Message Routing Header || GBT Header || Grouping Header || Response Payload || 0x40
1636 || SMD Signature
1637 It will be smaller than the Maximum PDU Size and so can be sent as a single APDU without
1638 any use of GBT. In this case it would have the following structure:
1639 Grouping Header || Response Payload || 0x40 || SMD Signature
1640 Example 3: small Command with large Response – e.g. read half-hourly profile (Export)
1641 The Command is:
1642 MAC Header || Grouping Header || read half-hourly profile (Export) Command Payload ||
1643 0x00 || ACB-SMD MAC
Page 90

SEC Schedule 8 – GBCS v4.4
1644 It will be smaller than the Maximum PDU Size and so can be sent as a single APDU without
1645 any use of GBT.
1646 The ESME Response is:
1647 MAC Header || Grouping Header || read half-hourly profile (Export) Response Payload ||
1648 0x00 || SMD-KRP MAC
1649 Assuming that there are 75 blocks to send the GBT Message Series would, if no retries are
1650 needed, be as follows:
1651 The ESME will send:
1652 Message Routing Header || GBT Header || Block 1
1653 …
1654 Message Routing Header || GBT Header || Block 63
1655 and wait for acknowledgement.
1656 The Access Control Broker will construct and send that acknowledgement whose structure
1657 is:
1658 Message Routing Header || GBT Header
1659 When this acknowledgement is received by the ESME, the ESME will send:
1660 Message Routing Header || GBT Header || Block 64
1661 …
1662 Message Routing Header || GBT Header || Block 75
1663 When the whole Message is received by the Access Control Broker, the Response can then
1664 be reconstructed:
1665 MAC Header || Grouping Header || read half-hourly profile (Export) Response Payload ||
1666 0x00 || SMD-KRP MAC
1667 Once the response has been reconstructed, the MAC can be checked.
1668 Device Requirements – DLMS COSEM
1669 Introduction – informative
1670 The DLMS COSEM server in the ESME and SAPC (and CHF where a DLMS COSEM server is
1671 present) responds to requests for information, and also provides Alerts in response to events
1672 within the Device (e.g. push data at the end of billing period; Alert in the event of a tamper;
Page 91

SEC Schedule 8 – GBCS v4.4
1673 disable supply when prepayment credit expires). To achieve this, a level of configuration is
1674 needed to ensure that the behaviour of the Device is as expected.
1675 The Technical Specifications require that the Critical Commands mandated by them (and so
1676 those defined in the GBCS) are the only Critical commands allowed. Devices may implement
1677 additional non Critical features only.
1678 The Technical Specifications only require DLMS COSEM certification on the ESME and the
1679 SAPC.DLMS COSEM objects (or functionality equivalent to them) are required to deliver the
1680 ESME / SAPC functionality defined in the Use Cases in a consistent way but should not be
1681 accessible via the Device’s HAN interface (i.e. it is internal functionality).
1682 General Requirements
1683 Constant values specified in Table 7.3.8a shall be fixed before operation and shall be
1684 immutable save via a firmware upgrade. This is to ensure consistent functioning and guard
1685 against potential attacks. Except where explicitly required by this Section 7.3, a Device shall
1686 not expose any part of any DLMS COSEM object, either for the writing of an attribute or for
1687 the invocation of a method that could, if used, constitute a Critical action.
1688 For Devices which are not ESME, SAPC or CHF (so where deviceType <> 1 or 2), the GBCS
1689 does not require the implementation of any DLMS COSEM objects.
1690 All Devices which are ESME (so where deviceType = 1):
1691 shall implement all of the DLMS COSEM objects, attributes and methods detailed in ‘SMETS
1692 Required Objects’ tab of the table in Section 20, and expose the specified attributes and
1693 methods over its network interface; and
1694 shall have the constant values set for the DLMS COSEM attributes specified as requiring
1695 constant values in Table 7.3.8a, and shall ensure that such values cannot be amended, save
1696 via activation of new firmware.
1697 All Devices which are SAPC (so where deviceType = 1):
1698 shall implement all of the DLMS COSEM objects, attributes and methods detailed in the
1699 ‘SMETS Required Objects’ tab of Table 20 which are:
1700 marked ‘mandatory’ in the ‘SAPC DLMS COSEM support’ column; or
1701 marked ‘optional’ in the ‘SAPC support’ column and are required for Use Cases that the
1702 SAPC does support,
1703 and shall expose such specified attributes and methods over its network interface;
1704 and
Page 92

SEC Schedule 8 – GBCS v4.4
1705 shall, where the SAPC supports the corresponding SMETS functionality, have the constant
1706 values set for the DLMS COSEM attributes specified as requiring constant values in Table
1707 7.3.8a, and shall ensure that such values cannot be amended, save via activation of new
1708 firmware.
1709 Application Associations
1710 An ESME, SAPC or CHF shall communicate using pre-established Application Associations
1711 (AA). These shall be set at manufacture, and the Device shall reject all subsequent attempts
1712 to open or release Application Associations.
1713 An ESME, SAPC or CHF shall support the Application Associations in Table 7.3.8c. An ESME,
1714 SAPC or CHF shall not support any additional Application Associations.
1715 The Application Associations in Table 7.3.8c shall limit access to DLMS features by
1716 configuring the object_list attribute to reflect the access granted to the role in ‘SMETS
1717 Required Objects’ tab of the Mapping Table in Section 20. For SAPC, the object_list attribute
1718 settings shall limit access in line with the ‘SMETS required objects’ tab of Table 20 to only
1719 those those rows which are either:
1720 marked ‘mandatory’ in the ‘SAPC DLMS COSEM support’ column; or
1721 marked ‘optional’ in the ‘SAPC DLMS COSEM support’ column and are required for Use
1722 Cases that the SAPC does support.
1723 Any other methods and attributes of any class shall be made inaccessible by listing them in
1724 the object_list attribute such that there is no access.
1725 The Public AA shall only expose:
1726 the SAP Assignment object; and
1727 the DLMS COSEM Logical Device name object and object_list with no objects listed other
1728 than the Association Logical Name (LN) Object (with its Blue Book meaning) and the SAP
1729 Assignment Object.
1730 When a Message is received by the Device, the Message shall be validated against the AA
1731 based on the Business Originator ID and the Message Code within the Grouping Header.
1732 Other attributes in the Association LN Objects and the Security Setup Objects shall be set at
1733 manufacture in accordance with Tables 7.3.8d and 7.3.8e.
1734 The ‘SAP Assignment’ object shall be configured at manufacture in accordance with Table
1735 7.3.8f. The method associated with the ‘SAP Assignment’ object shall not be accessible to
1736 any Application Association.

1766 Auxiliary Controller related scripts
1767 All italicised terms in this Section 7.3.6.1 shall have their DLMS COSEM meanings.
Page 94

SEC Schedule 8 – GBCS v4.4
1768 As required by DLMS COSEM, the execute method (method 1) of a script table object
1769 (class_id = 9) takes a long-unsigned value, so two octet value, as its parameter. To have an
1770 effect, the value of that long-unsigned parameter has to match one of the script_identfiers in
1771 that object’s scripts attribute (so attribute 2). Similar requirements apply to the
1772 script_selector values in schedule objects (class_id = 10).
1773 This Section 7.3.6.1 specifies the script_identifier values that SAPC and ESME shall support
1774 (and so the values such Devices shall accept in associated Use Cases) for script table objects
1775 with OBIS codes 0-0:10.0.103.255 and 0-0:10.0.107.255, and the functionality that such
1776 Devices shall implement when each such script_identifier in these two objects is executed.
1777 SAPC and ESME shall support all script_identifiers in objects 0-0:10.0.103.255 and 0-
1778 0:10.0.107.255 where:
1779 the most significant nibble of the most significant octet has a value of either 0x1, indicating
1780 output to the controlled load, or 0x2, indicating input;
1781 the least significant nibble of the most significant octet has a value of either 0x1, 0x2, 0x3,
1782 0x4 or 0x5, indicating ‘n’ in relation to Auxiliary Controller [n];
1783 for 0-0:10.0.103.255, the most significant bit of the least significant octet has a value of 0b0
1784 or 0b1;
1785 for 0-0:10.0.107.255, the most significant bit of the least significant octet has a value of 0b0;
1786 and
1787 the seven least significant bits of the least significant octet have a value between 0b0000000
1788 and 0b1100100 inclusive, so between 0 and 100.
1789 SAPC and ESME shall undertake the following processing based on the value of
1790 script_identifier, when a script in these script tables is invoked:
1791 where the most significant octet has a value of 0x1n, the Device shall only undertake any
1792 further script invocation processing where there is currently an Auxiliary Controller
1793 associated with Auxiliary Controller [n] and shall only undertake processing in relation to
1794 that Auxiliary Controller;
1795 where the most significant octet has a value of 0x2n, the Device shall only undertake any
1796 further script invocation processing where there is currently an Auxiliary Proportional
1797 Controller associated with Auxiliary Controller [n] and shall only undertake processing in
1798 relation to that Auxiliary Proportional Controller;
1799 where the script invocation is being requested as part of an ‘ECS47e Limit APC [n] Level’
1800 Command’s execution, the Device shall only undertake any further script invocation
Page 95

SEC Schedule 8 – GBCS v4.4
1801 processing where the currently associated Auxiliary Controller is an Auxiliary Proportional
1802 Controller;
1803 for 0-0:10.0.103.255, where the most significant bit of the least significant octet has a value
1804 of 0b1, the Device shall only take script invocation action where the script execution is being
1805 requested by the Auxiliary Controller Calendar (with its SMETS meaning) and so the schedule
1806 object with OBIS code 0-0:12.0.2.255;
1807 where the most significant bit of the least significant octet has a value of 0b0, the Device
1808 shall only take script invocation action where the script execution is being requested as part
1809 of an ‘ECS47a Set Auxiliary Controller [n] State’ or ‘ECS47e Limit APC [n] Level’ Command’s
1810 execution (so where the value of the data parameter in the execute method / the
1811 controllerNumberAndCommandedState field meets this requirement);
1812 where the preceding conditions are all met, the Device shall undertake processing for the
1813 commanded state of the Auxiliary Controller [n] according to the SMETS requirements, using
1814 the following interpretation of the seven least significant bits of the least significant octet
1815 and, where relevant, the most significant nibble of the most significant octet:
1816 for an Auxiliary Proportional Controller (with its SMETS meaning), the value of the seven
1817 least significant bits of the least significant octet shall be interpreted as a percentage
1818 between 0% (so 0b0000000) and 100% (so 0b1100100), which shall relate:
1819 to the output state, if the most significant nibble of the most significant octet is 0x1; or
1820 to the input state, if the most significant nibble of the most significant octet is 0x2;
1821 for an ALCS, the value of 0b1100100 in the seven least significant bits of the least significant
1822 octet shall be interpreted as meaning closure of the switch (so allowing energy to flow) and
1823 any other value shall be interpreted as meaning opening of the switch (so not allowing
1824 energy to flow); and
1825 for HCALCS, the value of 0b1100100 in the seven least significant bits of the least significant
1826 octet shall be interpreted as meaning closure of the switch (so allowing energy to flow) and
1827 so requiring the ‘Duty Cycle’ parameter in any resulting Load Control Event command to be
1828 0x64; any other value shall be interpreted as meaning opening of the switch (so not allowing
1829 energy to flow) and so requiring the ‘Duty Cycle’ parameter in any resulting Load Control
1830 Event command to be 0x00.
1831 Where that processing leads to a change in the commanded state of Auxiliary Controller [n],
1832 the Device shall update the Auxiliary Controller [n] State’s commanded state (so the value of
1833 either ‘p’ or ‘q’ in Section 7.2.9.2 and, where the Alerts are required by SMETS, the value of
1834 ‘resultingLevel’ in each of Use Cases ‘ECS101 Limit APC [n] Level Command processed’ and
1835 ‘ECS102 Limit APC [n] Level ended or cancelled’) to reflect the current commanded state:
Page 96

SEC Schedule 8 – GBCS v4.4
1836 where Auxiliary Controller [n] is an ALCS or HCALCS and its current commanded state is
1837 closure of the switch, ‘p’ and ‘q’ shall have the value 100. If its current commanded state is
1838 opening of the switch, ‘p’ and ‘q’ shall have the value 0; and
1839 where Auxiliary Controller [n] is an Auxiliary Proportional Controller, ‘p’ shall have a value
1840 between 0 and 100 inclusive, reflecting the percentage to which its commanded output
1841 state is currently set, ‘q’ shall have a value between 0 and 100 inclusive, reflecting the
1842 percentage to which its commanded input state is currently set.
1843 Correspondingly, as part of the step 4 checks in Section 6.2.4.1.1, Devices shall, for:
1844 script_selector values in Use Case ‘ECS46d Set Auxiliary Controller Calendar’ Commands; and,
1845 data values in the execute method of Use Case ‘ECS47a Set Auxiliary Controller [n] State’ /
1846 ‘ECS47e Limit APC [n] Level’ Commands,
1847 apply the following validation to each of those values:
1848 the most significant nibble of the most significant octet has a value of 0x1 or 0x2;
1849 the least significant nibble of the most significant octet has a value of either 0x1, 0x2, 0x3,
1850 0x4 or 0x5;
1851 the seven least significant bits of the least significant octet has a value between 0b0000000
1852 and 0b1100100 inclusive, so between 0 and 100; and
1853 for Use Case ‘ECS46d Set Auxiliary Controller Calendar’, the most significant bit of the least
1854 significant octet is 0b1; and
1855 for Use Cases ‘ECS47a Set Auxiliary Controller [n] State’ and ‘ECS47e Limit APC [n] Level’, the
1856 most significant bit of the least significant octet is 0b0.
1857 When creating an entry in the Auxiliary Controller Event Log (with its SMETS meaning) which
1858 relates to the execution of a script in objects 0-0:10.0.103.255 and 0-0:10.0.107.255, the
1859 Device shall record the script_identifier value in the
1860 entry_auxiliaryControllerLogEntry.switchNumberAndAction field of that log entry.

1862 Where an SAPC supports the related SMETS functionality, statements and requirements in
1863 this Section 7.3.7 shall apply to the SAPC as if it were an ESME.
1864 Summary of approach – informative
1865 As required by SMETS, an ESME has:
1866 a 1 * 48 matrix of primary element TOU (Time Of Use) consumption registers, and an
1867 associated 1 * 48 matrix of consumption based prices;
Page 97

1868  a 4 block by 8 time band matrix of primary element ‘TOU with Blocks’ consumption registers,
1869  and an associated 4 * 8 matrix of consumption based prices;
1870  a tariff switching table, which specifies time based switching between primary consumption
1871  registers and so between different prices.  (Switching between blocks is based on
1872  consumption passing thresholds and not on time);
1873  for Twin Element ESME only, a 1 * 4 matrix of secondary element TOU consumption registers,
1874  and an associated 1 * 4 matrix of consumption based prices; and
1875  for Twin Element ESME only, a secondary tariff switching table, which specifies time based
1876  switching between registers and so between different consumption based prices.
1877  There needs to be a clear mapping, at the level of encoded instructions in Commands to the
1878  ESME, between the switching table entries (identified by Script Selector), Consumption
1879  Registers and consumption based prices (identified by Index).  The next Section details that
1880  mapping for the encoded DLMS COSEM elements used by the ESME.
1881  Note that the mapping of Script Selector is included for information in Table 7.3.7.2, but the
1882  requirements for that mapping are in Section 7.3.8.

1904 ESME / SAPC accounts, credits and charges – informative
1905 Where an SAPC supports the related SMETS functionality, the statements in this Section
1906 7.3.9 apply to the SAPC as if it were an ESME.
1907 As detailed in the Mapping Table, an ESME shall have two Account objects (Class ID 111)
1908 which shall be used in both Credit and Prepayment Modes:
1909 a single ‘active’ Account object (OBIS code 0-0:19.0.0.255) which can be read in Use Cases
1910 but which is never written to directly; and
1911 a single ‘passive’ Account object (OBIS code 0-1:19.0.0.255) which can be written to in Use
1912 Cases but which is never read.
1913 Both relate to import energy.
1914 The activation attribute and method of the ‘passive’ object leads to its static values being
1915 copied from the passive to the active object, rather than the passive becoming active (see
1916 Section 9.2.2.7).
1917 The ‘Set Payment Mode to Credit’ and ‘Set Payment Mode to Prepayment’ Use Cases are
1918 used to trigger such activation of the ‘passive’ object. The SMETS attributes Suspend Debt
1919 Emergency and Suspend Debt Disabled are implemented as part of these objects and so are
1920 set in these Use Cases. If an ESME is in Prepayment Mode and the value of either Suspend
1921 Debt attribute is to be changed, this can be achieved by sending a Set Payment Mode to
1922 Prepayment Command containing the new values.

1925 7.3.10, an ESME and an SAPC, where it supports the related SMETS functionality, shall use the
1926 corresponding Specials Days Object in Table 7.3.10.

1928 Device requirements – ZSE
1929 This Section 7.4 details the ZigBee clusters, attributes and commands that shall be
1930 supported by Devices in their interactions with other Devices on the same HAN, including
1931 whether the support is as a ZSE client or a server. Note, this Section does not detail the ZCL
1932 / ZSE commands that Devices will need to process as part of processing Remote Party
1933 Commands, or Commands sent by a PPMID to a GSME. Such requirements are detailed in
1934 Sections 18 and 19.
1935 Only Devices capable of operating at Sub-GHz shall be required to support the requirements
1936 in rows of Table 7.4 where the cell in the column labelled ‘Sub GHz capable Devices only?’
1937 contains ‘Yes’.
1938 For clarity and as required by ZSE, all Devices shall support the Key Establishment Cluster as
1939 both Client and Server.
1940 A GSME shall implement a ZSE Metering Device and shall implement all the clusters,
1941 commands, attribute sets and attributes in Table 7.4 where column A is ‘GSME: Metering
1942 Device’.

1944 commands, attribute sets and attributes in Table 7.4 where column A is ‘GPF: Metering
1945 Device (Gas Mirror Endpoint)’.
1946 A GPF shall implement a ZSE Energy Services Interface and shall implement all the clusters,
1947 commands, attribute sets and attributes in Table 7.4 where column A is ‘GPF: Energy
1948 Services Interface (Gas ESI Endpoint)’
1949 A CHF shall implement a ZSE Remote Communications Device and shall implement all the
1950 clusters, commands, attribute sets and attributes in Table 7.4 where column A is ‘CHF:
1951 Remote Communications Device (Remote Communications Endpoint)’.
1952 An SAPC shall implement a ZSE Energy Services Interface and shall implement all the clusters,
1953 commands, attribute sets and attributes in Table 7.4 where column A is ‘SAPC: Energy
1954 Services Interface (Electricity ESI Endpoint)’.

SEC Schedule 8 – GBCS v4.4
2019 In some Use Cases, some attributes are marked as Encrypted.
2020 This Section 8 lays out requirements as to how such Encryption and related Decryption shall
2021 be undertaken.
2022 Approach – informative
2023 Since ZSE and DLMS have differing data types to represent the same attribute of SMETS
2024 information, there are some differences in the format of the data that is encrypted. These
2025 differences are laid out in this Section 8. However, Encryption and Decryption use the same
2026 cryptographic AES GCM primitives in the same way in all cases, regardless of protocol. The
2027 usage is the same as that to generate MACs for Remote Party Message protection, and
2028 therefore as per the AES GCM approach laid out in the Green Book.
2029 Encryption of SMETS attributes is required when:
2030 the Supplier reads the amounts held in Time Debt Register [1..2] and Payment Debt Register.
2031 Each of these is a single integer value;
2032 the Supplier reads the values held in the Active Import Register or Secondary Active Import
2033 Register or Consumption Register. Each of these is a single integer value;
2034 the Supplier reads the values held in the Tariff Block Counter Matrix, Tariff TOU Register
2035 Matrix or Tariff TOU Block Register Matrix;
2036 a Known Party or an Unknown Party reads one or more entries from a Log (with each entry
2037 in the specific log having a Log specific structure), specifically:
2038 the current or previous Supplier reads the Billing Data, the Daily Read Log (excluding the
2039 export related parts), or the Prepayment Daily Read Log. Note that a previous Supplier is an
2040 Unknown Remote Party as far as the meter is concerned;
2041 the Supplier, Network Operator, or an Unknown Remote Party reads the Daily Consumption
2042 Log or the Profile Data Log (Consumption parts);
2043 the Network Operator reads the Network Data Log;
2044 a Device sends an Alert containing a single entry from the Billing Data Log (excluding the
2045 export related parts).
2046 Common requirements
2047 All Encryption shall be Authenticated Encryption which:
2048 shall use the cryptographic primitives, input value structures and cryptographic material
2049 specified in Section 4; and
Page 108

SEC Schedule 8 – GBCS v4.4
2050 shall, for Key Agreement, use the Key Agreement key pair of the Device and the Remote
2051 Party which is accessing the data item.
2052 A Device shall, where it stores a data item listed in the Mapping Table as Encrypted, only
2053 provide that data in a Remote Party Message in Encrypted form.
2054 Where the Encrypted data item is within a Log, a Command requesting that data shall always
2055 have ‘from’ and ‘to’ date-times specified.
2056 Where all the octets in the ‘from’ date-time are 0x00 (excluding the least significant 3 bytes
2057 in Blue Book octet string formatted date-times), the Device shall interpret the ‘from’ field as
2058 meaning from the oldest in the Log.
2059 Where all the octets in the ‘to’ date-time are 0xFF (excluding the least significant 3 bytes in
2060 Blue Book octet string formatted date-times), the Device shall interpret the ‘to’ field as
2061 meaning to the newest in the Log.
2062 Where the Encrypted data item in the Mapping Table is not in a Log, a Command requesting
2063 that data shall never have ‘from’ or ‘to’ date-times specified.
2064 Key Derivation Inputs
2065 Where a Remote Party Message (1) contains Encrypted data items and (2) contains a
2066 Supplementary Remote Party ID, then the Encryption Remote Party shall be that identified
2067 by the Supplementary Remote Party ID. Otherwise, the Encryption Remote Party shall be
2068 the Remote Party identified in the Grouping Header of the Message.
2069 If the Message is to include a Supplementary Originator Counter generated by the Device
2070 (see Section 4.3.1.4), then the Encryption Originator Counter shall be the Supplementary
2071 Originator Counter. Otherwise the Encryption Originator Counter shall be the Originator
2072 Counter with the value in the Grouping Header of the Message.
2073 In relation to the Key Derivation Function requirements at Section 4.3.3, fields shall be
2074 populated as follows:
2075 ‘value of transaction-id’ shall be the concatenation 0x04 || Encryption Originator Counter.
2076 Note 0x04 ensures this value is not used in any other Key Derivation Function invocation
2077 save that related to this Encryption / Decryption; and
2078 for Encrypted data items in Responses and Alerts, ‘value of recipient-system-title’ shall be
2079 Encryption Remote Party and ‘value of originator-system-title’ shall be the Device’s Entity
2080 Identifier.
2081 AAD, Plaintext and Ciphertext
Page 109

SEC Schedule 8 – GBCS v4.4
2082 The Plaintext shall be set to the structure and content of the data item(s) as they would have
2083 been exposed on the Device’s HAN interface, if access to them were not constrained to be
2084 via Encrypted form by this Section 8.4.
2085 AAD shall be set to security control byte (SC) which shall have the value of 0x31 (see Section
2086 8.4.1).
2087 The Invocation Counter (IC) shall have a value of 0x00000000.
2088 The Authenticated Encryption MAC (AE MAC) shall be the MAC produced by applying
2089 Authenticated Encryption to AAD and Plaintext, as defined in NIST Special Publication 800-
2090 38D, with the values specified in this Section 8.4.
2091 Authenticated Encryption (AE) Ciphertext shall be the Ciphertext produced by applying
2092 Authenticated Encryption to Plaintext, with the values specified in this Section 8.4.
2093 Ciphered Information shall be the concatenation:
2094 SC || IC || AE Ciphertext || AE MAC
2095 Meaning of SC – informative
2096 The SC is set to 0x31 to reflect the following:
2097 Bits 3..0 are security suite which is 0b0001 since Security Suite 1 is required;
2098 Bit 4 is set to 0b1 since Authentication of the data is required;
2099 Bit 5 is set to 0b1 since Encryption of the data is required;
2100 Bit 6 is set to 0b0 since Messages containing the encrypted data are unicast; and
2101 Bit 7 is set to 0b0 as per the Green Book.
2102 Access to sensitive data – COSEM attribute access
2103 Access to sensitive data items shall be via the Data Protection class, as specified in the Blue
2104 Book. The required OBIS codes and associated details for each attribute shall be as specified
2105 in the ‘SMETS required objects’ tab in the Mapping Table.
2106 For clarity and in line with the Blue Book, the first octet of the plaintext input, constructed
2107 by the Device when using the Data Protection class, shall be 0x02 (the tag for structure
2108 according to Section 9.5 of the Green Book) and the next octet shall be the number of
2109 captured DLMS COSEM attributes in the Use Case.
2110 The Device shall only allow read access to attributes listed as Encrypted in the Mapping
2111 Table using the get_protected_attributes(data) method of the Data Protection class and not
2112 allow access to any other methods of such objects.
Page 110

SEC Schedule 8 – GBCS v4.4
|     |     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

2113  Values of the Data Protection class attributes
2114  The values of attributes 1, 3, 4, 5 and 6 of an object of the Data Protection class shall be set
2115  on a Device at manufacture, and those values shall not be capable of amendment except by
2116  firmware upgrade.  For each object of the Data Protection class:
2117  protection_object_list (attribute 3) shall be an array containing object_definition(s).  Within
2118  an object_definition: class_id, logical_name, attribute_index, data_index, restriction_type
2119  and restriction_value shall take values as per Table 7.3.8a;
2120  the value of protection_parameters_get (attribute 4) shall be a single entry array containing
2121  one protection_parameters_element, which shall have the values specified in Table 8.5.1;
